topic: Repeating a claim makes it feel true
subject: psychology

sources.title: Knowledge does not protect against illusory truth
The effects of repetition frequency on the illusory truth effect
The illusory truth effect leads to the spread of misinformation
The Trajectory of Truth: A Longitudinal Study of the Illusory Truth Effect
Repetition Increases Perceived Truth Even for Known Falsehoods
Limits of the illusory truth effect for social-political opinions: Evidence from two experiments and a mini meta-analysis

facts.claim: Prior knowledge does not protect against the illusory truth effect, even when the repeated false statement contradicts what a person already knows.
facts.quote: We again find that prior knowledge does not protect against the illusory truth effect. Repeated false statements were given higher truth ratings than novel statements, even when they contradicted participants’ prior knowledge.

facts.claim: People sometimes rely on fluency even if they already have knowledge available to them.
facts.quote: Multinomial modeling demonstrated that participants sometimes rely on fluency even if knowledge is also available to them (Experiment 2).

facts.claim: The illusory truth effect occurs even when repetitions happen minutes or weeks apart.
facts.quote: Contrary to some theoretical predictions, the illusory truth effect seems to be similar in magnitude for repetitions occurring after minutes or weeks.

facts.claim: Repetition does not significantly increase the perceived truthfulness of social-political opinion statements.
facts.quote: A mini meta-analysis combining the present findings with prior work further supported the conclusion that repetition effects for opinion statements are negligible within the tested bounds.

facts.claim: Repetition of misinformation makes people more likely to share it because it biases their judgment of accuracy.
facts.quote: the relationship between repetition and sharing was mediated by perceived accuracy. That is, repetition of misinformation biased people's judgment of accuracy and as a result fuelled the spread of misinformation.

facts.claim: The largest increase in perceived truth comes from encountering a statement for the second time, with smaller increases for each additional repetition.
facts.quote: The largest increase in perceived truth came from encountering a statement for the second time, and beyond this were incrementally smaller increases in perceived truth for each additional repetition.

research.angle: While repetition makes false facts feel truer even to people who know they are false, this effect does not appear to apply to social-political opinions.
research.verdict: Repetition increases perceived truthfulness for factual information by leveraging fluency, but this effect is limited by the type of content being presented.
research.caveat: The illusory truth effect may be stronger over shorter timescales and is notably less effective for evaluative or subjective opinions.
